steps.title: RGB Mini Project

quickCheck.question: Which set of Arduino Uno pins is used for PWM color control in this project?
quickCheck.explanation: Pins ~9, ~10, and ~11 all feature hardware PWM (tilde ~), allowing variable brightness on every color channel.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Look for the tilde (~) on the Uno silkscreen: pins 9, 10, and 11 all support PWM.

quickCheck.question: In the setColor(red, green, blue) function, what arguments produce a bright Yellow status light?
quickCheck.explanation: Yellow light is synthesized by mixing Red and Green while keeping Blue turned off.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: To create yellow light, turn ON Red (255) and Green (255), and set Blue to 0.

steps.title: Wiring 3 Current-Limiting Resistors
steps.markdownContent:
### Bench Rule: Three Separate Resistors!
Never share a single resistor on the common leg! If you do, turning on Red will steal current from Green, changing their brightness unevenly.

**Always put one 220Ω resistor on each individual color leg (R, G, and B)!**

steps.title: Build the RGB Mini Project Circuit
steps.markdownContent:
### Wire and Test
Wire pins 9, 10, and 11 to your RGB LED through 220Ω resistors and observe the color cycle.

steps.title: Mini Project Checkpoint
steps.markdownContent: Check your understanding of the concepts covered in this module.

questions.question: Why should each color channel have its own separate 220Ω protective resistor?
options: Different color diodes have different forward voltages and need independent current limits
questions.explanation: Red, green, and blue diodes have different forward voltages. Individual resistors prevent brightness interference!

questions.question: Which three Uno pins are commonly used for RGB PWM control?
questions.explanation: Pins 9, 10, and 11 are adjacent hardware PWM pins on the Uno header!
